listenings.text: Here is something that surprises almost every professional who learns English as an adult. In meetings, on calls and even in a lot of emails, native speakers rarely use the formal verb. Nobody says, let us postpone the meeting. They say, can we put it off? Nobody says, I will investigate the matter. They say, I'll look into it. The formal verbs are not wrong, and in a written contract they are exactly right. But in conversation they create a small distance, a sense that you are reading from a document instead of talking to a person. The good news is that you do not need hundreds of phrasal verbs. About twenty of them do most of the work in an office, and you probably know half of them already. The trick is to use the ones you know, on purpose, until they stop feeling like slang.

I have worked with British clients for about ten years, and the phrasal verbs I listen for most carefully are the soft ones. When a British colleague says, let me have a think and come back to you, the words are friendly and the meaning is often no. The same is true when they turn something down. A British manager will almost never say, we are turning down your proposal. They will say it is not quite what they are looking for at the moment, and they will expect you to figure out the rest. So when you hear a soft sentence with no decision in it, do not wait for the decision. Ask a short, neutral question. Is that something you would like us to set up, or should we put it to one side for now? Most people are relieved to be asked, and you will get the real answer in one sentence.
